Shorn of unnecessary details, the facts of the present Suit are that the Plaintiffs are the parents of a minor child namely Sunny, who was aged about four years at the time of the incident/accident, in respect of which damages have been claimed by way of filing of the instant suit. It has been averred in the plaint that on 29.06.2014, at about 07:00 PM to 07:30 PM, when the son of the Plaintiffs, namely Master Sunny, went to play in a nearby park (Indira Park, Gali No. 8, Shalimar Village, New Delhi) along-with other children of the locality, he suffered grievous injuries, due to leakage of electric current from an Air Cooler, installed by the Defendants. It has been stated that the Defendant No.1, was employed as a Chowkidar by the Defendant No. 2 /MCD, and that the Defendant No. 1 was residing in a pucca room, in the said public Park and one electricity meter was installed by the electric supply company (TPDDL), in order to supply electricity to the said pucca room. It is claimed that the Defendant No. 1 had in an negligent manner, installed an Air Cooler, outside the said pucca structure. That the minor son of the plaintiffs while playing in the said park, had come into contact with the stand of the said Air Cooler and due to the same, the son of the Plaintiffs, had received electric shock and resultantly, suffered severe burn injuries. That upon getting the information regarding the incident/ CS No.60273/16 Pooja & Anr. Vs. Lakhan Chowkidar & Ors. 2/23 accident, the Plaintiff No. 1, who is the mother of the minor had rushed to the Indira Park and after she reached at the spot of the incident, Plaintiff No. 1 found his son was lying and was sticked with an iron patti, which was fixed under the said Cooler stand. That the Plaintiff No. 1 somehow managed to separate his son from the said Cooler stand. It is further claimed that at that time, the Defendant No. 1 namely Lakhan Chowkidar, was found to be sitting on a chair on the other side of the room, by the Plaintiff No. 1 and that the Defendant No. 1 had spoken to the Plaintiff No. 1 and had said, "why have you taken out the boy, let him die, then only you will come to know". That subsequently, the matter was reported to local Police and one FIR bearing No.613/14, PS Shalimar Bagh, Delhi was also lodged against the Defendant No. 1, in respect of the offence punishable under section 337 IPC and the said FIR / matter was stated to be pending trial on the date of filing of the suit. 3. texts.arguments: 6. By Replication, the plaintiff has reiterated that statutory notice as was required in terms of DMC Act, was duly served upon the Defendant No. 2/ MCD. That the Plaintiffs, were not having any callous attitude and there was no negligence on the part of the plaintiffs, as was claimed by the Defendants. That the accident/ incident in question was not attributable to the negligent conduct of the plaintiffs. 22. During the course of final arguments, it was vehemently argued on behalf of both the Defendants, by their respective Counsels that the present suit is not maintainable as the same has been filed by the parents of the injured child for compensation, in their own name and not in the name of the minor injured child, especially when the same could have been filed in accordance with the rules contained in Order 32 CPC. It has been argued that the cause of action to claim damages is personal in nature and a suit on the basis of the said cause of action, can only be filed by the person himself, who had suffered injuries, in his own name, as a Plaintiff and not by any other person. At the same time, the parents of the said injured person have no right to institute a suit to claim damages, on behalf of their own child, as has been CS No.60273/16 Pooja & Anr. Vs. Lakhan Chowkidar & Ors. 16/23 done, in the instant case. On the strength of these arguments, prayer was made on behalf of the Defendants to dismiss the instant suit, being non- maintainable. Negligence means failure to exercise due care expected from a reasonable prudent person. Negligence implies breach of duty or lack of proper care in doing CS No.60273/16 Pooja & Anr. Vs. Lakhan Chowkidar & Ors. 17/23 something. In short, it is want of attention and doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would or would not do. Clerk & Lindsell on Torts (18th Ed.) sets out four requirements of the tort of negligence and the same read: (1) the existence in law of duty of care situation, i.e. one in which the law attaches liability to carelessness. There has to be recognition by law that the careless infliction of the kind of damages in suit on the class of per- son to which the claimant be longs by the class of person to which the de- fendant belongs is actionable; (2) breach of duty of care by the defendant, i.e. that it failed to meas- ure up to the standard set by law; (3) a casual connection between the defendant's careless conduct and the damage; (4) that the particular kind of damage to the particular claimant is not so unforeseeable as to be too remote." 26. In the opinion of this court, the facts of the instant suit speak for themselves and the principle of res ipsa loquitur applies with full force, in these facts. In this context reference may be had to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as Shyam Sunder & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan, (1974) 1 SCC 690, where the concept of res ipsa loquitur was explained. The relevant portion of the said judgment reads as follows:- (2) Sh. Vijay Singh vs (1) Sh. Lakhan Chowkidar on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/97362530/ 11 "10. The maxim is stated in its classic form by Erle, C.J.: [Scott v. London & St. Katherine Docks, (1865) 3 H&C 596, 601] "... where the thing is shown to be under the management of the defendant or his servants, and the accident is such as in the ordinary course of things does not happen if those who have the management use proper care, it affords reasonable evidence, in the ab- sence of explanation by the defendants, that the accident arose from want of care." The maxim does not embody any rule of substantive law nor a rule of evidence. It is perhaps not a rule of any kind but simply the caption to an ar- gument on the evidence. Lord Shaw remarked that if the phrase had not been in Latin, nobody would have called it a principle [Ballard v. North British Rail- way Co., 1923 SC (HL) 43]. The maxim is only a convenient label to apply to a set of circumstances in which the plaintiff proves a case so as to call for a re- buttal from the defendant, without having to allege and prove any specific act or omission on the part of the defendant. The principal function of the maxim is to prevent injustice which would result if a plaintiff were invariably com- pelled to prove the precise cause of the accident and the defendant responsible for it even when the facts bearing on these matters are at the outset unknown to him and often within the knowledge of the defendant. But though the par- ties' relative access to evidence is an influential factor, it is not controlling. Thus, the fact that the defendant is as much at a loss to explain the accident or himself died in it, does not preclude an adverse inference against him, if the odds otherwise point to his negligence (see John G. Fleming, The Law of Torts, CS No.60273/16 Pooja & Anr. Vs. Lakhan Chowkidar & Ors. 19/23 4th Edn., p. 264). The mere happening of the accident may be more consistent with the negligence on the part of the defendant than with other causes. The maxim is based as common sense and its purpose is to do justice when the facts bearing on causation and on the care exercised by defendant are at the outset unknown to the plaintiff and are or ought to be within the knowledge of the defendant (see Barkway v. S. Wales Transo [(1950) 1 All ER 392, 399] ). 11. The plaintiff merely proves a result, not any particular act or omis- sion producing the result. CS No.60273/16 Pooja & Anr. Vs. Lakhan Chowkidar & Ors. 22/23 Issue No. 2:- (II) Whether the present suit is barred by the provisions of Section 477/478 of the DMC Act?
